text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementEnvironmentWhy Are These Polar Bears Thriving?Our writer journeys to northern Canada to investigate an environmental paradoxEKBy Elena Kazamia9:00 AM CST on November 21, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIt was my turn to watch for polar bears, though I wasn’t entirely sure what watching for one on a hot beach in summer was supposed to look like. Around me, on a tiny island in James Bay in Quebec, Canada, the field team moved with practiced efficiency, unspooling barbed wire and setting up a camera trap. I found an elevated spot on the warm ground, and periodically glanced over my shoulder at the dense, low-slung pine forest behind us. Arctic terns darted like paper planes above our heads. Beluga whales crested against the horizon.“Don’t worry, the bears are probably asleep right now,” Harry Erless, squinting into the midday sun, assured me. Erless, gregarious as he is knowledgeable, is an experienced ranger and trapper of the Cree Nation of Waskaganish, an Indigenous community on the southeast shore of James Bay.This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus.To get it in print, join by Nov 30.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
